source.title: Single-Bit-per-Weight Deep Convolutional Neural Networks without Batch-Normalization Layers for Embedded Systems
source.authors: Mark D. McDonnell; Hesham Mostafa; Run-Chun Wang; A. Schaik

record.tranche_reason: Compares BN and BN-free training behavior and reports whether training diverges, converges slowly, or proceeds like the baseline; it does not measure accuracy over time.
record.gate_note: The paper reports CIFAR and ImageNet test-error tables, but those final test errors do not measure the training speed named in V6. Its explicit training-behavior statements do bear on V6. The BN-free recipe uses shifted ReLUs and, for the fully BN-free case, a temperature scaling layer.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own qualitative convergence and learning-rate comparisons after removing BN from wide residual networks. These bear on V6 in a new architecture and weight-precision setting, although accuracy gain over training time is not measured.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors conclude that the accuracy penalty from replacing BN depends on dataset, network size and weight precision, and that retaining only final BN often reduces that penalty. They also report that final BN or constant output scaling permits use of the baseline training recipe and high initial learning rate. Complete BN removal was evaluated on CIFAR; ImageNet retained final BN.
record.recipe_differences: Compares BN with shifted-ReLU replacements and a final temperature-scaling layer; does not use Fixup's initialization, scalar biases, or multipliers.
record.method_sensitivity: Training behavior depends on whether a final BN or temperature-scaling layer is present; without BN, lower learning rates were a partial remedy but slowed convergence and increased error rates. Temperatures below approximately 30 tended to fail to converge shortly after training commenced.
record.peer_reviewed: Asia-Pacific Conference on Intelligent Robot Systems
record.problems: Training-behavior evidence is qualitative: no time-to-accuracy values, run counts, or uncertainty are stated for the divergence and convergence observations. The reported test-error tables do not measure training speed.
record.rows_left_out: Tables I–III and Figures 5–6 report final test error rates, not training speed or convergence timing, so they do not measure V6's stated training-speed outcome. No other result rows were left out.

untested.parts: Training classification error, random or corrupted labels, and model-size or stopping effects on training fit.
Teacher-student ReLU optimization, spurious local minima, and extra student neurons.
Depth-related training degradation and comparisons of plain networks with identity-shortcut networks.
Comparative initialization effects on training speed, signal propagation and trainable depth.
Initial stability thresholds, catapult recovery, curvature and edge-of-stability dynamics.
Measured accuracy gain over time or time to a target accuracy; the original sigmoid, VGG and Inception settings; and Fixup's specific initialization, biases and multipliers.

record.verdict_notes: Convergence evidence is qualitative and lacks training curves, run counts or uncertainty for these observations. Final test-error tables cannot establish training speed. The alternative recipe changes activations and output scaling, so its success qualifies BN's necessity without isolating the effect of BN alone.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, random or corrupted labels, model-size effects on fitting, and early stopping are not tested.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student local minima and student width are not tested.
Plain versus residual networks and depth-related training error are not compared.
Initialization comparisons and signal or gradient propagation across depth are not tested.
Learning rates above the stability limit and curvature or sharpness behavior are not tested.
Does not report time-to-accuracy measurements or compare against Fixup. It tests BN removal using shifted ReLUs and temperature scaling, rather than Fixup's recipe.

rows.subject: wide residual networks
rows.size_stated: CIFAR: depth 20, widths 4× and 10×; ImageNet: depth 18, widths 1× and 2.5×
rows.operation_detail: Train with BN layers; paper reports this as the baseline recipe.
rows.value: Baseline training recipe; the paper says BN enables a larger initial learning rate.
rows.note: Qualitative statement about training behavior; no speed or time-to-accuracy value is given.
rows.check: This row combines a baseline training recipe with a literature statement from Section II-A. Neither independently measures a BN benefit; retain the recipe as comparator metadata rather than a result row.

rows.subject: wide residual networks
rows.size_stated: CIFAR: depth 20, widths 4× and 10×; ImageNet: depth 18, widths 1× and 2.5×
rows.operation_detail: Remove all BN layers and replace them with shifted ReLUs; reduce learning rate as a partial remedy.
rows.baseline: BN networks allow a larger initial learning rate.
rows.value: Training diverged or converged very slowly; reducing the learning rate was a partial remedy but led to slow convergence and increased error rates.
rows.note: The text does not quantify runs or the degree of divergence or slow convergence.
rows.check: Slow convergence or divergence without BN, and slower convergence after reducing the learning rate, support the stated BN advantage; 'partial' incorrectly describes the remedy rather than the claim's effect. Section III-D does not identify which dataset, width or precision exhibited each outcome, so the row must not imply separate confirmation for every listed model.

rows.subject: wide residual networks
rows.size_stated: CIFAR: depth 20, widths 4× and 10×; ImageNet: depth 18, widths 1× and 2.5×
rows.operation_detail: Use a single final BN layer with other BN-ReLU combinations replaced by shifted ReLUs.
rows.value: A single BN layer at the end enabled training exactly like the baseline models.
rows.note: Qualitative comparison; no time-to-accuracy measurement is given.
rows.check: Relative to the full-BN baseline, no training-recipe or learning-rate advantage was reported when only the final BN layer remained. This qualifies the need for distributed BN, but does not establish measured equality of accuracy gain over time. ImageNet tested this final-BN variant, not complete BN removal.

rows.subject: wide residual networks
rows.size_stated: CIFAR: depth 20, widths 4× and 10×; ImageNet: depth 18, widths 1× and 2.5×
rows.operation_detail: Replace the final BN layer with constant scaling, implemented as softmax temperature scaling.

conditions.value: same high initial learning rate as baseline

rows.value: Temperature scaling enabled training to take place identically to the baseline models, including the same high initial learning rate.
rows.note: The text says lower temperatures tended to fail to converge shortly after training commenced.
rows.check: The full-BN baseline's learning-rate advantage disappeared with shifted ReLUs and temperature scaling; 'observed' reverses the direction relative to V6's BN-benefit comparison. Restrict complete BN removal to CIFAR experiments: ImageNet compared baseline BN with final-BN-only networks. Input-channel normalization was retained as preprocessing.

tranche.reason: Own convergence and learning-rate results test V6 in wide residual networks with full-precision and binary weights, a new architecture and precision setting.

source_check.notes: Complete internal BN removal was evaluated on CIFAR; ImageNet comparisons retained final BN. Input-channel normalization remains as preprocessing; training-speed comparisons are qualitative.

statements.correction: Section III-D: final BN permits the baseline training recipe; output temperature approximately 30–100 permits baseline-like training with the same high initial learning rate. Figures 5–6 show final accuracy spreads across repeated runs.
statements.problem: Baseline-like trajectories overstates the evidence: the study reports qualitative training behavior and recipe compatibility, without learning curves establishing matched accuracy trajectories.
